title: Format IELTS: True / False / Not Given
topic: Membedakan pernyataan yang benar, salah, atau tidak disebutkan dalam teks
objectives: Membedakan True, False, dan Not Given dengan dasar teks
Mengenali pernyataan yang bertentangan dengan teks
Tidak menebak informasi yang tidak disebut

block1.tip: True berarti teks mengatakan hal yang sama. False berarti teks mengatakan kebalikannya. Not Given berarti teks tidak menyebutkannya sama sekali.

lesson.intro: Dalam soal True, False, Not Given, kamu hanya boleh memakai informasi dari teks. Jangan memakai pengetahuanmu sendiri, dan jangan menebak apa yang mungkin benar.

sections.heading: True dan False
sections.bodyMd: Jawab **True** jika pernyataan sejalan dengan teks. Jawab **False** jika pernyataan **contradict** isi teks. Perhatikan kata seperti only, all, dan always, karena sering membuat pernyataan menjadi salah.

sections.heading: Not Given
sections.bodyMd: Pilih **Not Given** jika teks tidak menyebut hal itu. Pernyataan yang masuk akal belum tentu ada di teks. Jika teks hanya menyebut topiknya, itu belum cukup untuk **True**.

sections.heading: Hati-hati dengan klaim dan asumsi
sections.bodyMd: Sebuah **claim** harus diperiksa. Jika teks memberi **assumption** yang belum diuji, pernyataan yang bergantung padanya bisa menjadi **Not Given**. Gunakan kata kerja **verify** dalam pikiranmu: apa buktinya di teks?

block3.title: Perdebatan Jalur Sepeda
block3.text:
The city council published a statement about the new bicycle lanes on Hill Street. According to the statement, the lanes reduced accidents by forty percent in one year. The mayor repeated this claim in a television interview, and many newspapers printed it the next day.

However, a local researcher said the claim would contradict the traffic reports she had reviewed. Her team counted accidents for two years, before and after the lanes were built. They found a smaller drop, closer to fifteen percent. The researcher argued that the council had not explained how the forty percent figure was calculated.

The council's official reply was that the figure used a different time period. This explanation is possible, but the council did not publish the data. Without the full data, it is difficult to verify which number is correct. Readers should be careful, because a partial figure can mislead people even when it is not false.

Some critics went further. They claimed that the council wanted to distort the results to win support for its next project. Other people believed the lanes were a clear success, because cyclists now use the street every morning. Both views rely on assumptions that were never tested. The assumption that more cyclists means fewer accidents is valid in some cities, but it does not automatically hold everywhere.

The researcher did not say that the lanes were a failure. Her report stated only that the reduction was smaller than the council had claimed, and she warned that her sample covered only one district. She also noted that the number of cyclists had grown by a third, which may have added risk at busy corners. This detail was unstated in the council's announcement.

Journalists sometimes exaggerate good news, and this story was no exception. A headline that said 'Bike lanes save lives' was not supported by the evidence in the report. A more careful headline would have said that accidents fell, but by less than first reported.

In the end, the council agreed to publish the full dataset next month. Until then, the debate remains open, and the claim cannot be fully confirmed by the public. Several residents have also asked for an open meeting, where the figures can be discussed in detail with local experts.
